read: full: abstract, sections 1-6 (p.1-9), Appendix A (literature), B (datasets, including B.3 on EngTrace, p.14-16), C.1-C.2 (models, prompts) and D.2.2 (robustness on FinChain and EngTrace, p.23-25), Table 13 and Figure 24 (p.34); the remaining appendix figures and tables skimmed. The text file contains some non-UTF-8 bytes and needs 'grep -a'.
venue_now: arXiv preprint 2605.15393v1 [cs.LG], 14 May 2026, with 'Date: May 18, 2026' on p.1 (FAIR at Meta, LMU Munich); no venue shown, though the acknowledgments thank 'the anonymous reviewers' (p.10).
what_it_is: LPDS (logic-preserving difficulty scaling) is a method, not a benchmark. It estimates how hard a symbolic-template variation is for a given model, by the Mahalanobis distance of the response's hidden states from the model's own correct responses to other variations of the template, or by Levenshtein distance. It then runs a beam search over the template's variable slots for the hardest variations (p.1, p.4-7). It is applied to 100 templates each from GSM-Symbolic, FinChain and EngTrace (the May release, taken from its public GitHub repository), with 5-shot CoT and final-answer scoring (p.3-4, p.16). Searched variations expose more failures than random sampling: on GSM-Symbolic the drop against GSM8K is up to about 5 times larger (p.1, p.7). EngTrace variations are the hardest of the three sets for the three small models run on them (p.24-25, p.34). Fine-tuning on harder variations gives more consistent gains (GSM-Symbolic and FinChain only, p.9).
domain: robustness evaluation on symbolic templates: grade-school math (GSM-Symbolic), finance (FinChain), engineering (EngTrace: chemical, electrical, mechanical)
size: 100 templates per dataset; 1,000 variations per template (100,000 per dataset) to validate the difficulty metrics (p.5); beam search with T = 15, b = 16, w = 16 (p.6). Seven open models from 3B to 72B in total (p.3, p.17), but only Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B are reported on EngTrace (Figure 9b p.24, Table 13c p.34).
source_of_items: perturbed from an existing set: existing symbolic templates (GSM-Symbolic, FinChain, EngTrace) with extended variable lists and restricted numeric ranges. EngTrace templates whose variables change the solution structure were split into separate templates, and 100 were selected (p.15-16).
instances: generated: variations instantiated from templates and selected adversarially by beam search (p.6-7)
has_gold_traces: partial: the templates' ground-truth reasoning is used only as fine-tuning targets (p.9). The difficulty metrics compare a response with the model's own correct responses to other variations, not with gold traces (p.4).
evaluation: final answer: the last number after '####' is extracted by regex; exact match for GSM-Symbolic, and for FinChain and EngTrace a tolerance of 1e-6 + 1% relative (p.4). Difficulty metrics are judged by AUC and odds ratio for predicting correctness (p.5). No step-level evaluation.
human_validation: none reported; only a qualitative look at responses as difficulty rises (p.6) and the authors' own template splitting (p.16).
contamination_measures: perturbations: symbolic variations are presented as revealing 'performance inflation due to data contamination and reliance on superficial patterns' (p.2-3, p.8). No measure of its own.

engtrace_use.explanation: Candidate; the May paper does not cite it. LPDS uses EngTrace's May templates (Gull et al., 2025, arXiv 2511.01650) as one of its three datasets (p.3, p.16). Its introduction names EngTrace's practice of evaluating 'a randomly sampled subset of instances (Xie et al., 2025; Gull et al., 2025)' as one that 'can overestimate robustness' (p.2), a criticism that still applies to the revised pool, whose instances are drawn round-robin rather than searched.

suggested_wording: Evaluating symbolic templates on randomly sampled instances can overstate robustness: LPDS (Mondorf et al., 2026) searches each template's logic-preserving variations for the hardest ones and finds accuracy drops up to five times larger than under random sampling, and its engineering templates are the hardest of its three template sets for the small models it tests.
facts_to_cite: LPDS scores a variation's difficulty by the Mahalanobis distance of the response's hidden states from the model's correct responses to other variations, and searches template variables by beam search for the hardest variations (p.4-7)
Applied to 100 templates each from GSM-Symbolic, FinChain and EngTrace (p.3)

On GSM-Symbolic, accuracy drops relative to GSM8K are up to about five times larger on searched variations than on random samples (e.g. Qwen-2.5-72B: 9.0 against 2.2 points) (p.1, Figure 5b p.7, text p.8)

On EngTrace, beam-searched variations raise error rates over random samples for Llama-3.2-3B (74.3% against 69.2%), Llama-3.1-8B (69.5% against 63.7%) and Qwen-2.5-7B (49.9% against 42.6%) (Figure 9b, p.24)
Performance drops 'fastest and most substantially' on EngTrace variations; difficulty-robustness scores 0.24 to 0.51 on EngTrace against 0.54 to 0.90 on GSM-Symbolic (p.25, Table 13 p.34)
Existing symbolic-template evaluations, EngTrace included, 'typically assess models on a randomly sampled subset of instances', which 'can overestimate robustness' (p.2)
Some EngTrace templates contain variables that change the solution structure, and LPDS split them into separate templates (p.16)
Fine-tuning on harder variations gives more consistent robustness gains (shown on GSM-Symbolic and FinChain) (p.9)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: symbolic templates and generated instances (it uses EngTrace's own May templates, p.3, p.16); a final-answer check with a relative tolerance (p.4); a robustness question close to EngTrace's paraphrase arm. Lacks, as a method rather than a benchmark: any process-level or step-level evaluation (final answer only, p.4); use of gold traces in evaluation; expert validation; large models on EngTrace (three models of 3B to 8B). What EngTrace must say in response: its instances are a stratified draw (round-robin over reasoning-path and answer-form groups from the first 100 draws), not an adversarial search, so its scores are average-case estimates that LPDS-style search could lower. Its paraphrase test probes wording, not adversarial choice of values. Its process-level checks address what LPDS does not measure.
notes: (1) Surprise for the authors: Figure 24 (p.34) reproduces an EngTrace template under the old name 'EngChain Template', and its last gold step reads 'sin(sqrt({initial_vel_ms} / {mass} * t)' where 'sin(sqrt({stiffness} / {mass}) * t)' is expected; the stiffness range '{1000, 1001, ..., 19999, 200000}' also looks garbled. Either LPDS mis-transcribed the template or the released May template (undamped spring-mass, displacement x(t) at t = 2) has a defect in its gold reasoning text; the team should check the public repository and the current template. (2) LPDS took the 90 May templates from a public GitHub repository (p.16, footnote 4). The private seed (D-114) hides instance values, but the logic and gold procedure of those 90 templates were public, so the revised contamination claim should be worded with that in mind. (3) LPDS found templates whose variables switch the solution structure (p.16); this matches the state brief's reasoning-path groups and is worth naming when describing the round-robin sampling. (4) The batch note's 'accuracy falls fastest on EngTrace variations' is accurate (p.25) but rests on three small models. (5) Anonymity: how to describe LPDS's use of the May release without signalling authorship is the authors' decision.
